children.text: Testing, one, two, three, four. [background conversation]
Mi tía, era Vidal. [Translation: My aunt, she was a Vidal]
Era Vidal, de los Villareals si, si.  [Translation: She was Vidal, of the Villareals yes.]

Sí. Mi tía Benita cumple años hoy y cumple 90 años, mi hermana está en una fiesta en su casa. Mi mamá cuando era joven iba a los bailes de Narciso Martinez y decía que-
[Translation: Yes. My aunt Benita's birthday is today, she is 90 years old, my sister is at a party at her house. My mom when she was young went to the dances of Narciso Martinez and she said that- ]
El Huracán del Valle. [The Hurricane of the Valley]

Sí, El Huracán del Valle, y dice que ya los conocía a usted, a su familia y usted...
 [Translation: Yes, The Hurricane of the Valley, and she said that she knew you, your family and yourself...]
Cuando quiera Doctor.  [Translation: Whenever you are ready Doctor.]

Dr. Paredes, I have a few questions and this is just to fill in the information that we had here in the last interview. Now, the first one you've already answered, your father moved to Brownsville in 1904?
Could you give us a little bit about why he moved and-

It's too long a story but you can always cut it. [laugh] My father was always a rebel, he was the oldest of the family, and therefore he was supposed to inherit the old home place as he called it, but three times-- The fourth one was when he did come to Brownsville, he tried to rebel.

The very first one was when he was a young boy, there was an outlaw band around and he joined it in an old horse. His next oldest brother would tell me about that, he was the one that inherited the old home place.
What was his name?

Vicente. My youngest son-- No, this is the old one, he's named Vicente for him because I used to go to Tío Vicente's ranch in summers and that's where I learned the corridos and became very much involved in our history, in our folklore.

My father, as I say, he ran away that time, he didn't get very far because his horse wasn't in good shape, it was an old horse. After the Rurales chased the band a while they caught up with him, they brought him back to my grandfather. The second time he ran away to Monterrey

and he did pretty well financially until he got ill. He had very, very severe pain in his legs so they brought him home and after his father forgave him he was okay. The third time has more historic significance, he joined Catarino Garza's revolt against Díaz, he was wounded.

Of course, his father had fought against the French, he was a supporter of Díaz, so they arranged for things to be settled. So he came home and apparently had decided to stay here, he built a house just across the road from where my grandfather lived and he married, and his first children were born

in the rancho when around 1904 he finally just decided he would move to Brownsville, he took his family to Brownsville. I imagine, of course, I don't know exactly the details, that he and his father were estranged for a while but then that was settled and he stayed in Brownsville,
and did pretty well there. I have a picture around there of my father and mother in 1914, he had been 10 years already in Brownsville.
In the previous interview you made mention of the first time you heard the word mojado, do you remember when that was and how old you were?

I was in grammar school. The revolution was still going on and one of the little boys were out in the playground, and one of the little boys was being chased by other boys was, kids can be rather cruel sometimes. They finally caught up with him, knocked him down, and felt under behind his ears
because if he was a mojado his ears would be wet so this business about 'wetbacks' came much later. I think probably it was that I might have mentioned.
Yes, exactly, I didn't know when you had heard it yet.

In fact that when I finished junior college I started working for the Brownsville Herald and James Frank Dobie, was at the height of his popularity and he appeared in the paper a great deal. One time he described the origin of the word "wetback"

because mojado didn't translate very well into English, especially since those are the prohibition times and wets meant those were for alcohol, the dries were against it. Somebody cooked up that name, "wetback", and Dobie apparently, this is what the paper said, gave the etymology

of the word wetback. The Mexicans would cross the river, and no this isn't my comment, apparently they were too dumb to take their clothes off, they would cross the river completely dressed, then when they to this side they were tired, so what does a Mexican do? He would lie down on his back

and he would sleep, the sun would dry him out except for his back, so when he got up his back would be wet. I don't know whether you're familiar with my novel George Washington Gómez , there I satirized poor Dobbie mercilessly. Later I met him and he wasn't a bad guy.
Very interesting, so it was during your grammar school years that you heard it for the first time?
Yes, that was when a lot of refugees were coming over they were not from just across the river because people just cross the river, we didn't think of them as mojados, they were our own people.
What year did you graduate from high school, Dr. Paredes?
1934, and from Brownsville Junior College in 1936?
Good. Last time we spoke you said that when you were in Brownsville junior college there were three Mexicanos-Americanos and they were called El Flaco, El Chaparro, y El Grandote?
Yes.
Could you give us little information about why they got their names and what kind of relationship the three of you had?
I was El Flaco, you can look at me and see I'm still El Flaco.

El Chaparro was Roberto Ramirez, his father I think was named Don Florentino Ramirez. I think one of Roberto's brothers probably lives in Brownsville, Elías Florentino Junior, and he was shorter, much shorter than I was. El Grandote was Sabas Klahn, K-L-A-H-N.

He seemed huge to us then though later here he was visiting us here, he was standing against the door and I said, "Me parece que encogiste," [Translation: It appears you shrank,] and he says, "No, I always been," "How tall?" he says, "5'11," but 5'11 was very tall usually at that time. We three were inseparable in junior college.
How many Mexican-American students were there at the college?

Very few, I think they were I can remember two, or three, women. The one that remained with me because I knew her later was Berta Cabaza, she was from San Benito, she became a teacher, a very good teacher. There were probably a couple
more but the ones that were stuck together we all were aspiring writers, and so on, were Roberto Ramirez, Sabas Klahn. Roberto and Sabas are both dead now.
When was the first time you met Reynaldo Garza?

In school, in high school, I remember. In fact, he may have been already, because Sabas went to St. Joseph's academy but Reynaldo was in classes that I took because the high school level you take classes-- You might be where the classes might have juniors and seniors,
and I think Reynaldo was a senior when I was a junior.
This was at Brownsville high school [Americo: Yes]
You had told us previously that you used to sing for local radio station? What was the name of that station and what are your recollections of that?
I have no idea what the name. It started with a K, of course, all of them.
Yes, all of them. [laughter] That wouldn't be KBOR?
Was that one in Brownsville?
That was in Brownsville for a long time, KBOR, but that's-

That may have been it, because this was this was in the '30s, the second half of the '30s. Yes, I sang, I began singing my own songs and then the Cardenas', rather the youngest of the sons, got the idea of sponsoring 15 minutes and I would sing mostly my own songs, and for $15 a week, 15 minutes.
I always like to say that once I had a job before I earned $1 a minute [chuckles]
Which was pretty good money back then, is that correct?
Oh, yes, and I was working for The Herald.
Yes, that was at the same time, very good. I don't think we went over this question the last time but I have a question for you, what is your advice to young people who want to - [video cuts]
